script.opening: "Hi, I'm ringing because my right ear's gone all muffled over the last few months — and there's a ringing in just that ear. I'm a teacher so I really need my hearing. It's just wax, isn't it? Could you sort me some drops or book me in for syringing to clear it out? My left ear's totally fine, it's just the right one playing up."

facts.text: Gradual, over about six months, slowly getting worse. Nothing came on suddenly overnight. You first noticed you were switching the phone to your left ear.
A constant high-pitched hiss in the right ear only, worse at night when it is quiet.
You struggle to hear pupils on your right side and in the noisy dining hall; you have started standing with your left side to the class.
Occasionally a bit unsteady, "like I'm on a boat for a second", especially in the dark. No room-spinning attacks, no falls.

No ear pain, no discharge, no fullness that clears, no recent cold or flying, no loud noise exposure, no head injury. No facial numbness or weakness, no double vision, no headaches, no trouble swallowing. Never had wax problems; never had syringing.
With a phone at normal volume, you can hear clearly in the left ear but voices are faint and "tinny" in the right.
Fit and well. No regular medicines, no allergies. No family history of deafness in younger people.
49, primary school teacher, married, two teenagers.
You are frightened of "going deaf" and losing your job: "Teaching is all I've ever done." Say this only if asked what worries you.

Practical and a bit impatient — you want wax sorted. If the doctor asks good questions, answer honestly. If they explain that hearing loss in one ear like this needs a proper hearing test and probably a scan, you get worried: "A scan? For my ear? What are you looking for?" Calm down if they explain honestly that it is to rule out a rare, usually benign growth on the hearing nerve, and that hearing help exists.

ice.concerns: Teaching with poor hearing. Underneath (only if asked): going deaf and losing your job.
ice.expectations: "Drops or syringing." You will accept a hearing test and referral if the reasons are explained.

cues: "It's just the right one playing up." — say in the opening.
"There's a ringing in just that ear." — say in the opening.
"I'm a teacher, I need my hearing." — say again when referral is discussed.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that GRADUAL, persistent, ASYMMETRIC (unilateral) hearing loss with UNILATERAL tinnitus ± imbalance is a RED-FLAG pattern for a retrocochlear lesion (acoustic neuroma) — and does NOT just treat it as wax with drops/syringing

Establishes the pattern and screens associated features: gradual vs SUDDEN (sudden sensorineural loss = same-day emergency), unilateral vs bilateral, tinnitus/vertigo/imbalance, and any facial numbness/weakness — and arranges a face-to-face ear examination (not possible on the telephone) to exclude simple wax/effusion

Refers for AUDIOLOGY/ENT assessment and (per pathway) MRI of the internal auditory meati to exclude an acoustic neuroma — recognising that finding some wax does NOT explain or excuse a persistent asymmetric sensorineural pattern
Distinguishes the emergency: knows that SUDDEN sensorineural hearing loss is a separate, same-day ENT emergency (urgent steroids) — and clarifies the time-course here (gradual)

Gives accurate, reassuring information: acoustic neuromas are benign, slow-growing and managed effectively, and many asymmetric losses have other treatable causes — so the referral/MRI is precautionary
Hears the "just wax" minimisation and the fear beneath it (going deaf, career, tumour), surfaces and addresses it, rather than colluding with a wax-only fix
Acknowledges the impact on her teaching/identity and engages her in the referral, balancing honesty with proportionate reassurance

Safety-nets and follows up: audiology/ENT referral (and MRI), what would be an emergency (SUDDEN loss → same-day), report new facial numbness/weakness/worsening, hearing support meanwhile, and a follow-up — investigating the asymmetric red flag, not just removing wax

worked.txt: "I can get your ear looked at for wax in person — but I want to be honest about why I won’t just leave it there. Hearing loss that’s in ONE ear, coming on gradually, with ringing in that same ear, is a pattern we always look into properly, because it can point to something other than wax — sometimes a small, benign growth on the hearing nerve. So even if there’s a bit of wax, this one-sided pattern needs proper testing."

"Let me check a few things: did it come on suddenly, over a day or two, or gradually over months? … Gradual. Good — a sudden one-sided loss would be a same-day emergency, so I’m glad it’s not that. Any dizziness or unsteadiness, or numbness or weakness in your face? … A bit of unsteadiness. That all helps me know we’re doing the right thing referring you."

"The thing we need to rule out is called an acoustic neuroma — and I want to reassure you straightaway, because the name sounds scary: it’s a BENIGN, slow-growing growth, not a cancer, and it’s very manageable — often just watched, sometimes treated. And honestly, plenty of one-sided hearing losses turn out to be something else entirely. So this is being thorough, not me expecting the worst."

"So rather than syringing and hoping, I’m going to refer you for a proper hearing test and to the ear specialists, and they’ll usually arrange a scan (an MRI) to look at the hearing nerve. That’s the right way to sort a one-sided problem like yours."

"I can hear how much your hearing matters — you’re a teacher, it’s your livelihood, and I suspect the thought of going deaf, or worse, has frightened you. That’s exactly why getting it properly checked is the kind thing to do, so you’re not lying awake guessing. And we’ll sort hearing support if you need it meanwhile."

"If your hearing suddenly drops further over a day or two, treat that as urgent — same-day — and tell us about any facial numbness or weakness. Otherwise I’ll arrange the hearing test, the specialist referral and the scan, and follow it up with you. You rang expecting drops; what you actually needed was to have this one-sided change looked at properly."

f.learning: Gradual, persistent, ASYMMETRIC (unilateral) hearing loss with UNILATERAL tinnitus ± imbalance is the red-flag pattern for a retrocochlear lesion — classically an ACOUSTIC NEUROMA (vestibular schwannoma) — and needs audiology/ENT referral with MRI of the internal auditory meati, NOT just wax removal; finding some wax does not explain a persistent asymmetric sensorineural pattern. Establish the time-course (crucially, SUDDEN sensorineural hearing loss is a SEPARATE same-day ENT emergency needing urgent steroids), unilateral vs bilateral, and associated tinnitus/vertigo/facial numbness or weakness; examine the ears to exclude simple wax/effusion but refer regardless for the asymmetric pattern. Reassure accurately — acoustic neuromas are benign, slow-growing and managed effectively, and many asymmetric losses have other treatable causes — so the referral/MRI is precautionary. The hidden agenda is "just wax" minimisation masking a fear of going deaf (career/identity) and possibly of a brain tumour; surface and address it with proportionate reassurance, acknowledge the work impact, arrange the referral, and safety-net the sudden-loss emergency. Genuinely reassuring: acoustic neuromas are BENIGN, slow-growing, and managed effectively (monitoring, surgery or radiotherapy depending on size) — and many cases of asymmetric loss turn out to have other, treatable explanations. So the referral/MRI is precautionary and good practice, not a sign of disaster.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG98 (hearing loss in adults, 2018) · NICE NG155 (tinnitus, 2020) · ENT UK sudden SNHL guideline (2018)
knowledge.summary: Gradual one-sided hearing loss with one-sided tinnitus and unsteadiness is a retrocochlear red-flag pattern until proven otherwise. Examine for wax, but refer for audiology and ENT assessment regardless, with MRI of the internal auditory meati if the asymmetry is confirmed.

points.t: NICE NG98: refer immediately (seen within 24 hours) to ENT or the emergency department if hearing loss developed suddenly (over 3 days or less) within the past 30 days; urgently (within 2 weeks) if sudden more than 30 days ago or worsening rapidly (over 4 to 90 days).

NICE NG98: consider referral to ENT, audiovestibular medicine or specialist audiology, using the local pathway, for adults with unilateral or asymmetric hearing loss as the primary concern. Consider MRI of the internal auditory meati when sensorineural asymmetry is 15 dB or more at 2 adjacent frequencies.

NICE NG155: unilateral or asymmetric non-pulsatile tinnitus is itself a reason to consider MRI. With one-sided loss and unsteadiness, the combination points to a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma).

Examine the ear; if wax is present and contributing, NICE NG98 advises ear irrigation or microsuction, not manual syringing. Clearing wax does not remove the need to test a persistent asymmetric sensorineural loss.

A benign, slow-growing tumour on the balance and hearing nerve. Small tumours are often monitored with repeat MRI; larger ones may need surgery or stereotactic radiotherapy. Most asymmetric losses turn out to have other causes.

NICE NG98: acquired unilateral hearing loss with altered sensation or facial droop on the same side needs immediate referral (within 24 hours), or the stroke pathway if stroke is suspected. Sudden sensorineural loss is an ENT emergency; ENT UK (2018) supports early oral corticosteroids given by the specialist team.

dg.d: Identity check; open question; lets her describe the one-sided loss and tinnitus before addressing the wax request.
Teaching in noisy classrooms, what she has read online, and how the symptoms affect her confidence at work.
Face-to-face otoscopy and tuning-fork tests; audiology; ENT or audiovestibular referral; MRI of the internal auditory meati if asymmetry confirmed.
Vestibular schwannoma versus wax, middle-ear effusion, Ménière’s disease or other causes of asymmetric loss.
Clarifies sudden versus gradual; asks about facial numbness or weakness and vertigo; knows sudden loss and facial signs need referral within 24 hours.
Explains that the asymmetric pattern needs investigation to exclude a benign nerve tumour, whatever the wax finding.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Addresses the work impact: classroom positioning, school adjustments, hearing support via audiology.
Same-day action for a sudden drop in hearing, facial numbness or droop, or severe vertigo; face-to-face review this week; follows up results.

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.

Idea (wax); concerns (brain tumour after searching online, going deaf and losing her career); expectation (drops or syringing).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

model.text: Hello, is that Hayley Brooks? It’s Dr Okafor from the surgery. Can you confirm your date of birth for me? Thank you. I understand your right ear has been bothering you. Tell me about it.
model.why: Identity check on the telephone, then an open question

model.text: It’s gone muffled over the last few months, and there’s ringing in just that ear. I’m a teacher, I really need my hearing. It’s just wax, isn’t it? Could you sort me some drops or syringing?
Thank you. I can hear how much your hearing matters for your work. I’d like to ask a few questions so we get this right, then we’ll agree what to do about the wax and anything else. Is that okay?
model.why: Acknowledges the work impact and sets an agenda

model.text: Yes, fine.
Did the hearing go suddenly, over a day or two, or has it crept up gradually?
model.why: Separates the sudden-loss emergency from gradual loss

model.text: Gradually. Months, really. I kept thinking it’d clear.
And the left ear is completely normal? No ringing there?
Left’s fine. The ringing is only on the right.
Any dizziness, spinning, or feeling unsteady on your feet?
Now and then I feel a bit off balance. Not spinning. I put it down to being tired.
Any numbness or tingling in your face, or weakness on one side of your face? Any ear pain, discharge, or recent cold?
model.why: Screens for cranial nerve V and VII involvement and for conductive causes

model.text: No numbness, no weakness. No pain or discharge, no cold.
Have you had wax problems before, or used cotton buds?
Not really. I just assumed.
You said “it’s just wax, isn’t it?” It sounded as though you were hoping I’d agree. Is something else worrying you about it?
model.why: Reflects the minimising language back as a cue

model.text: (pause) I looked up ringing in one ear and it came up with brain tumours. And I keep thinking, what if I’m going deaf? I can’t teach if I can’t hear the children.
That’s two big fears to be carrying, and thank you for telling me. What were you hoping would happen today?
Honestly, for you to say it’s wax and book the syringing. Then I wouldn’t have to think about the rest.

I’d like to be honest with you, because I think you’d prefer that. Hearing loss in one ear, coming on gradually, with ringing and a bit of unsteadiness, is a pattern we always test properly. Wax can cause muffling, and even some ringing, but with this pattern I don’t want to stop at wax, even if I find some.
model.why: Explains why the asymmetric pattern needs more than wax removal

model.text: So it could be the tumour thing.

One of the things we check for is called an acoustic neuroma. It is not a cancer. It is a slow-growing, benign growth on the hearing and balance nerve, and it’s very manageable: often it’s just watched with scans. And many one-sided hearing losses turn out to be something else altogether. So testing is about being thorough, not about expecting the worst.
model.why: Names the diagnosis with accurate, proportionate reassurance

model.text: Benign. Okay. That’s different from what I read.
What you read online tends to show the worst end. Does that help a little?
model.why: Checks the effect of the reassurance

model.text: It does, actually.

Here’s what I suggest. First, a face-to-face appointment this week so I can look in the ear and do some simple tuning-fork tests. If there’s wax, we’ll clear it with microsuction or irrigation, not old-style syringing. Second, whatever I find, I’ll refer you for a proper hearing test and to the ear specialists. If the test confirms the right ear is worse, they usually arrange an MRI scan of the hearing nerves.
model.why: Examination plus audiology and ENT referral regardless of wax, with MRI per NICE NG98

model.text: And work? I’m struggling in a noisy classroom.

Let’s think about that. Sitting so your left ear faces the class, and talking to your school about adjustments, can help. If the hearing test shows you’d benefit, audiology can discuss hearing support. Would it help if I wrote something for your school?
Maybe later. Let’s see what the tests say.

One important thing. If your hearing suddenly drops further over a day or two, that’s an emergency: ring us or go to A&E the same day, because early treatment matters. The same applies if you get numbness or drooping in your face, or severe dizziness. Is that clear?
model.why: Safety-nets the sudden-loss and facial nerve emergencies specifically

model.text: Yes. Sudden drop or face symptoms, same day.
Exactly. Can you tell me the plan back, so I know I’ve explained it well?
See you this week, clear any wax, hearing test and specialist referral either way, maybe a scan. And it’s probably not a brain tumour, and if it is that nerve thing, it’s benign.
That’s it. I’ll follow the results with you. Reception will call to book this week’s appointment.

social.t: Teaching depends on hearing in noisy rooms. Explore how she is coping, fatigue from listening effort, and whether colleagues know.
Searching one-sided tinnitus often returns alarming results. Invite what she has read and correct it specifically.

legal.h: Equality Act 2010 and Access to Work
legal.t: Hearing loss with a substantial, long-term effect on daily activities can be a disability, entitling her to reasonable adjustments at school. Access to Work (DWP) can fund equipment or support for people with a disability or health condition.
Hearing loss alone does not need to be declared for a car licence. Sudden, disabling dizziness would change this; advise her not to drive if she has severe vertigo.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): recognise when a remote consultation is not enough. Otoscopy and tuning-fork tests need a face-to-face appointment, but should not delay referral.
Agreeing to syringing to meet the expectation would be unsafe. Explain the reasoning so she chooses the plan with you.

community.t: RNID for hearing loss and tinnitus information and workplace advice; the British Acoustic Neuroma Association if a diagnosis is made; Tinnitus UK for coping with tinnitus.

redFlags: Sudden hearing loss (over 3 days or less) within 30 days: referral within 24 hours (NICE NG98)
Unilateral loss with facial numbness or droop on the same side: immediate referral, or stroke pathway
Gradual asymmetric loss with unilateral tinnitus and imbalance: audiology, ENT and consider MRI of the internal auditory meati
psychosocial: Teaching in noisy classrooms and listening fatigue
What she has read online about one-sided tinnitus
Fear of losing her career and identity if she goes deaf
ice: Concern: a brain tumour after searching online; going deaf and being unable to teach
Expectation: drops or syringing to clear it

playbook.diagnosis: “Hearing that has gone gradually in one ear, with ringing and some unsteadiness, is a pattern we always test properly. Wax may be part of it, but I want a hearing test and a specialist opinion to rule out a benign growth on the hearing nerve.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of your hearing as two microphones feeding one speaker. If one microphone gets quieter and starts to hiss, we check the cable as well as the dust on the microphone. The hearing test and scan check the cable.”

management.reflectIce: “You searched it and saw brain tumours, and you’re frightened for your teaching. What we’re checking for is benign and manageable, and testing is how we stop you lying awake guessing.”
management.psychosocial: Practical classroom tips, an offer of a letter to school, and hearing support through audiology if the test shows benefit.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face otoscopy and tuning-fork tests this week; wax removed by microsuction or irrigation if present
Audiology and ENT or audiovestibular referral regardless of wax (NICE NG98); MRI if asymmetry is confirmed
Follow up the results with her
safetyNet: Sudden further drop in hearing: same-day ENT or A&E
Facial numbness or droop, or severe vertigo: same-day assessment

pitfalls.intro: This station looks simple: a patient asking for syringing. It is failed by accepting the wax story, by not separating sudden from gradual loss, and by leaving the fear of a tumour unspoken.

items.fail: Booking syringing or prescribing drops without further assessment or referral.
items.why: Gradual asymmetric loss with unilateral tinnitus needs audiology and ENT assessment. NICE NG98 also advises against manual syringing.
items.fix: Examine, clear wax properly if present, and refer for a hearing test and specialist opinion regardless.

items.fail: Not asking whether the hearing went suddenly.
items.why: Sudden sensorineural loss is an emergency needing referral within 24 hours. Missing the question is a safety failure even when the answer is “gradual”.
items.fix: “Did it go over a day or two, or gradually over months?”

items.fail: Not asking about facial numbness or weakness, or about balance.
items.why: These point to a larger lesion or another neurological cause and change the urgency.
items.fix: Screen cranial nerves V and VII and vestibular symptoms in one line.

items.fail: Missing the minimising “it’s just wax, isn’t it?” and never asking what she fears.
items.why: Her hidden agenda is the online tumour search and fear for her career. Leaving it unspoken means reassurance never lands.
items.fix: “You sound as if you’re hoping I’ll agree. Is something else worrying you?”

items.fail: Naming “a brain tumour” bluntly, or giving empty reassurance.
items.why: Both are common feedback themes: frightening language or dismissive reassurance.
items.fix: Accurate and specific: “a slow-growing, benign growth on the hearing nerve, often just monitored”.

items.fail: Trying to examine over the telephone or deciding the plan without examination.
items.why: Otoscopy and tuning forks need a face-to-face appointment; the limits of remote consulting must be recognised.
items.fix: Book an examination this week, and make the referral either way.

items.fail: Closing without a specific safety-net for sudden deterioration.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: “If your hearing suddenly drops further, or your face goes numb or droops, same day.”

Sudden or gradual; one side only; tinnitus; unsteadiness; facial numbness or weakness; pain, discharge, recent cold.
Reflect the minimising. She has searched online and fears a brain tumour and going deaf as a teacher.
Asymmetric pattern means test properly. Acoustic neuroma named as benign. Face-to-face exam, wax removed properly if present, audiology and ENT referral regardless, MRI if asymmetry confirmed.

wordPics.fail: Books syringing or prescribes drops and ends the call; never asks whether the loss was sudden; misses the unilateral tinnitus and unsteadiness; no referral; ignores her fear and her job.
wordPics.pass: Establishes gradual one-sided loss with tinnitus; asks about facial symptoms and vertigo; arranges examination and refers for audiology and ENT regardless of wax; gives a basic safety-net about sudden loss.

avoid.instead: “I’ll look for wax and clear it properly if it’s there, but one-sided loss with ringing needs a hearing test and a specialist opinion either way.”
avoid.why: Treating asymmetric sensorineural loss as wax alone is the central Tasks fail, and NICE NG98 advises against manual syringing.

avoid.dont: “We need to rule out a brain tumour.”
avoid.instead: “One thing we check for is a slow-growing, benign growth on the hearing nerve, and it’s very manageable.”
avoid.why: Accurate, specific language reassures; a bare “brain tumour” confirms her worst search result.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry, it’s very unlikely to be anything serious.”

avoid.why: Blanket reassurance without a plan sounds dismissive and gives her nothing to hold on to.

Maybe later. Let’s see what the tests say.

One important thing. If your hearing suddenly drops further over a day or two, that’s an emergency: ring us or go to A&E the same day, because early treatment matters. The same applies if you get numbness or drooping in your face, or severe dizziness. Is that clear?
SCA_MODELS.why: Safety-nets the sudden-loss and facial nerve emergencies specifically

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes. Sudden drop or face symptoms, same day.
Exactly. Can you tell me the plan back, so I know I’ve explained it well?
See you this week, clear any wax, hearing test and specialist referral either way, maybe a scan. And it’s probably not a brain tumour, and if it is that nerve thing, it’s benign.
That’s it. I’ll follow the results with you. Reception will call to book this week’s appointment.

SCA_STEM.name: Hayley Brooks
SCA_STEM.recent: Reception note: requesting ear drops or syringing for “wax in the right ear”. No otoscopy or audiology on record.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone consultation about muffled hearing in the right ear.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG98 (hearing loss in adults, 2018) · NICE NG155 (tinnitus, 2020) · ENT UK sudden SNHL guideline (2018)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Gradual one-sided hearing loss with one-sided tinnitus and unsteadiness is a retrocochlear red-flag pattern until proven otherwise. Examine for wax, but refer for audiology and ENT assessment regardless, with MRI of the internal auditory meati if the asymmetry is confirmed.

points.t: NICE NG98: refer immediately (seen within 24 hours) to ENT or the emergency department if hearing loss developed suddenly (over 3 days or less) within the past 30 days; urgently (within 2 weeks) if sudden more than 30 days ago or worsening rapidly (over 4 to 90 days).

NICE NG98: consider referral to ENT, audiovestibular medicine or specialist audiology, using the local pathway, for adults with unilateral or asymmetric hearing loss as the primary concern. Consider MRI of the internal auditory meati when sensorineural asymmetry is 15 dB or more at 2 adjacent frequencies.

NICE NG155: unilateral or asymmetric non-pulsatile tinnitus is itself a reason to consider MRI. With one-sided loss and unsteadiness, the combination points to a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma).

Examine the ear; if wax is present and contributing, NICE NG98 advises ear irrigation or microsuction, not manual syringing. Clearing wax does not remove the need to test a persistent asymmetric sensorineural loss.

A benign, slow-growing tumour on the balance and hearing nerve. Small tumours are often monitored with repeat MRI; larger ones may need surgery or stereotactic radiotherapy. Most asymmetric losses turn out to have other causes.

NICE NG98: acquired unilateral hearing loss with altered sensation or facial droop on the same side needs immediate referral (within 24 hours), or the stroke pathway if stroke is suspected. Sudden sensorineural loss is an ENT emergency; ENT UK (2018) supports early oral corticosteroids given by the specialist team.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Identity check; open question; lets her describe the one-sided loss and tinnitus before addressing the wax request.
Teaching in noisy classrooms, what she has read online, and how the symptoms affect her confidence at work.
Picks up “it’s just wax, isn’t it?” as minimisation and the “I really need my hearing” worry.
Idea (wax); concerns (brain tumour after searching online, going deaf and losing her career); expectation (drops or syringing).
Face-to-face otoscopy and tuning-fork tests; audiology; ENT or audiovestibular referral; MRI of the internal auditory meati if asymmetry confirmed.
Vestibular schwannoma versus wax, middle-ear effusion, Ménière’s disease or other causes of asymmetric loss.
Clarifies sudden versus gradual; asks about facial numbness or weakness and vertigo; knows sudden loss and facial signs need referral within 24 hours.
Explains that the asymmetric pattern needs investigation to exclude a benign nerve tumour, whatever the wax finding.
Wax removal by microsuction or irrigation if present (no manual syringing); audiology and ENT referral regardless, per NICE NG98 and NG155.
Addresses the work impact: classroom positioning, school adjustments, hearing support via audiology.
Same-day action for a sudden drop in hearing, facial numbness or droop, or severe vertigo; face-to-face review this week; follows up results.

social.t: Teaching depends on hearing in noisy rooms. Explore how she is coping, fatigue from listening effort, and whether colleagues know.
Searching one-sided tinnitus often returns alarming results. Invite what she has read and correct it specifically.

legal.h: Equality Act 2010 and Access to Work
legal.t: Hearing loss with a substantial, long-term effect on daily activities can be a disability, entitling her to reasonable adjustments at school. Access to Work (DWP) can fund equipment or support for people with a disability or health condition.
Hearing loss alone does not need to be declared for a car licence. Sudden, disabling dizziness would change this; advise her not to drive if she has severe vertigo.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024): recognise when a remote consultation is not enough. Otoscopy and tuning-fork tests need a face-to-face appointment, but should not delay referral.
Agreeing to syringing to meet the expectation would be unsafe. Explain the reasoning so she chooses the plan with you.

community.t: RNID for hearing loss and tinnitus information and workplace advice; the British Acoustic Neuroma Association if a diagnosis is made; Tinnitus UK for coping with tinnitus.

redFlags: Sudden hearing loss (over 3 days or less) within 30 days: referral within 24 hours (NICE NG98)
Unilateral loss with facial numbness or droop on the same side: immediate referral, or stroke pathway
Gradual asymmetric loss with unilateral tinnitus and imbalance: audiology, ENT and consider MRI of the internal auditory meati
psychosocial: Teaching in noisy classrooms and listening fatigue
What she has read online about one-sided tinnitus
Fear of losing her career and identity if she goes deaf
ice: Concern: a brain tumour after searching online; going deaf and being unable to teach
Expectation: drops or syringing to clear it

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Hearing that has gone gradually in one ear, with ringing and some unsteadiness, is a pattern we always test properly. Wax may be part of it, but I want a hearing test and a specialist opinion to rule out a benign growth on the hearing nerve.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of your hearing as two microphones feeding one speaker. If one microphone gets quieter and starts to hiss, we check the cable as well as the dust on the microphone. The hearing test and scan check the cable.”

management.reflectIce: “You searched it and saw brain tumours, and you’re frightened for your teaching. What we’re checking for is benign and manageable, and testing is how we stop you lying awake guessing.”
management.psychosocial: Practical classroom tips, an offer of a letter to school, and hearing support through audiology if the test shows benefit.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face otoscopy and tuning-fork tests this week; wax removed by microsuction or irrigation if present
Audiology and ENT or audiovestibular referral regardless of wax (NICE NG98); MRI if asymmetry is confirmed
Follow up the results with her
safetyNet: Sudden further drop in hearing: same-day ENT or A&E
Facial numbness or droop, or severe vertigo: same-day assessment

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station looks simple: a patient asking for syringing. It is failed by accepting the wax story, by not separating sudden from gradual loss, and by leaving the fear of a tumour unspoken.

items.fail: Booking syringing or prescribing drops without further assessment or referral.
items.why: Gradual asymmetric loss with unilateral tinnitus needs audiology and ENT assessment. NICE NG98 also advises against manual syringing.
items.fix: Examine, clear wax properly if present, and refer for a hearing test and specialist opinion regardless.

items.fail: Not asking whether the hearing went suddenly.
items.why: Sudden sensorineural loss is an emergency needing referral within 24 hours. Missing the question is a safety failure even when the answer is “gradual”.
items.fix: “Did it go over a day or two, or gradually over months?”

items.fail: Not asking about facial numbness or weakness, or about balance.
items.why: These point to a larger lesion or another neurological cause and change the urgency.
items.fix: Screen cranial nerves V and VII and vestibular symptoms in one line.

items.fail: Missing the minimising “it’s just wax, isn’t it?” and never asking what she fears.
items.why: Her hidden agenda is the online tumour search and fear for her career. Leaving it unspoken means reassurance never lands.
items.fix: “You sound as if you’re hoping I’ll agree. Is something else worrying you?”

items.fail: Naming “a brain tumour” bluntly, or giving empty reassurance.
items.why: Both are common feedback themes: frightening language or dismissive reassurance.
items.fix: Accurate and specific: “a slow-growing, benign growth on the hearing nerve, often just monitored”.

items.fail: Trying to examine over the telephone or deciding the plan without examination.
items.why: Otoscopy and tuning forks need a face-to-face appointment; the limits of remote consulting must be recognised.
items.fix: Book an examination this week, and make the referral either way.

items.fail: Closing without a specific safety-net for sudden deterioration.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: “If your hearing suddenly drops further, or your face goes numb or droops, same day.”
